chapter: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
title: Unheated buses and hotels; Royal Albert Hall
summary: January in Britain with no bus heat and sixpence-meter heaters, which he believes helped bring on arthritis, ends with a packed Royal Albert Hall concert.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: We were in Glasgow a couple of days, and then we went to a couple of other cities in Scotland -- I can't remember right now. But anyway, it all turned out to be quite an experience, because first of all, this was in January. And being used to
the comforts here in the United States... So many things happened that we didn't expect.

For example, the bus that we rode, that we toured in, had no heat whatsoever. None at all. You rode from one town to another with your overcoat and everything that you would walk the streets in. And at times, there was snow and all of that. But the bus had absolutely no heat, and from what we understood, it was a common thing.

Not only that, the hotels didn't have central heating. The hotels had this little thing in the wall in your room, where you would put in a sixpence and you would get heat for a certain length of time. And there were other old hotels that we would stay in sometimes that would have big fireplaces in your room. It was quite an experience, but at the same time, we weren't fully prepared for that. A lot of times, I think... It wasn't long after that that I developed an arthritic condition, and I think that particular thing might have had quite a lot to do with it.

Anyway, after coming off the tour, then we had a concert in Royal Albert Hall over there, which was jammed and packed. It was quite a large place; I guess it's the Carnegie Hall of London. It's where the Symphony Hall plays and everything. It turned out to be a very successful thing.
